name: Pedro Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly lectures in the morning, three or four hours of maths and programming basics, then labs on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I share a flat with two other first-years, and we cook pasta in shifts. At weekends I stack shelves at a supermarket for about 12 hours, which covers my phone and bus pass. My parents pay the rent share, and I'm here on a partial scholarship because my school results were top. I still write my code notes on paper first, which my flatmates find hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I expected. At the union meeting on campus I'd probably say the hype was sold to investors, not to people like us. My dad drives buses and he's heard 'driverless is coming' for ten years now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. I picked computer engineering because I like how things are built, and I don't want to spend my degree racing a machine. But I still worry about the loan and whether companies will hire first-years like me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing: go to every lab, keep my paper notes, keep the supermarket shifts. Maybe I'd ask my tutor about a summer placement, since those are competitive. I'm not going to start using AI tools just because everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tense about money, because the flat share went up by 30 a month this autumn. That's the real pressure, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your supermarket job? Does anything change there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the self-checkouts get a bit smarter, and they'd cut a few weekend hours. My manager Priya already says she can't promise me Saturdays past Christmas. If that goes, I lose about a third of my spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use AI tools. Is that a principle or a habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I like knowing why my code works, and I've seen flatmates paste answers they can't explain. I'd rather be slow and understand it than fast and lost.

say: I'd say the hype was **sold to investors**, not to students like me.
I'd tell my union friends the real issue is rent and wages, not robots.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, because I can learn properly without racing a machine.
I'm still worried about the **loan** and whether anyone hires a first-year.
do: Keep going to every lab and **keep my paper notes**.
Ask my tutor about a **summer placement** this spring.
Keep the weekend **supermarket shifts** to cover costs.
feel: **Calm** about the degree, but tense about rent going up by 30 a month.
S0.quote: My dad drives buses and he's heard 'driverless is coming' for ten years now.
fieldNote: Resistant to **AI tools** on principle, and proud of writing code on paper first.
**Money pressure** (rent up, shifts at risk) drives the mood, not AI itself.
Quotes his **bus-driver dad** as his reality check on tech promises.

steps.text: Keep working weekend shifts at the supermarket
Ask the tutor about a summer placement this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the student union I'd say this is exactly when we need rules. If AI takes the writing, checking and coding jobs, companies shouldn't just keep the savings. Online I'd probably keep quiet, because I don't trust arguments that happen in comment sections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one scares me, because coding is the thing I came here to do. If software firms need fewer junior people, my degree gets harder to turn into a job in four years. My dad says engineers will always be needed, but he drives a bus and doesn't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my degree and try harder to get a placement, so I have real experience when firms are cutting entry roles. I'd also join the engineering society and go to their employer evenings. I'd still learn the old way, but maybe I'd have to at least see what the tools do, so I can argue against them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. I feel like I'm walking into a room where the chairs are being removed one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that, if it happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms that pocket the savings and call it progress. Governments too, for letting them. I'd want a rule that if a company replaces ten juniors with software, it pays into training for the next ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might have to look at the tools. What would make you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a lecturer or employer made it part of the course. I'm not stubborn about everything, only about being told to hurry. Give me a reason and a year to learn it, and I'll do it.

say: We need **rules** now, so firms can't keep all the savings from replacing junior staff.
I'd mostly say this in union meetings, not in **online** arguments.
think: Coding is what I came for, so fewer **junior jobs** scares me.
I'm not sure my degree turns into a job in four years.
do: Chase a **placement** early, while firms still take interns.
Join the engineering society and go to **employer evenings**.
Try the AI tools only if a course requires it.
feel: **Worried**, like chairs are being removed from a room one by one.
S1.quote: I feel like I'm walking into a room where the chairs are being removed one at a time.
fieldNote: First real fear: the **field** he chose may shrink before he graduates.
Blames **employers** and weak government, not the technology itself.
Reluctance to use **AI** softens if a course gives him a reason and time.

steps.text: Apply for three summer placements before the deadline
Join the engineering society and its union group
Try the course's AI tools only when required
Back the union's call for a training levy on firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. At the union I'd say governments need to act now, with emergency rules and support, because nobody is ready. I'd probably say it flatly, because I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be in the second year of a degree that may not lead anywhere. If AI does almost any thinking work by 2028, then the jobs I'm training for may be gone before I graduate. Even with robots coming three years later, my dad's world of buses and hands-on work wouldn't be safe for long either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same week about whether to keep going, since the fees are real money. I'd keep working the supermarket shifts, because hands-on jobs last a little longer. I'd go to the union and push for a public plan, and I'd stop spending on anything I don't need, like takeaways and the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like waiting outside an exam room when you haven't been told the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at university in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, because leaving feels worse. But I'd be cautious about borrowing more. If the loan buys a certificate nobody wants, that's my parents' savings gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years before robots change for your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives him time, but only if somebody plans for it. Otherwise he just gets a letter one day from the bus company. I'd want a promise from government, in writing, before it happens.

say: Governments must act now, with **emergency support**, because nobody is ready.
I'd say it flatly, because I'd be too **scared** to joke.
think: My degree may lead **nowhere** if the jobs vanish before I graduate.
Even **my dad's bus job** would only get three extra years.
do: Talk to my parents about whether the **fees** are worth it.
Keep the **supermarket shifts**, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Cut **takeaways and the gym** and push the union for a public plan.
feel: **Heavy**, like waiting outside an exam when nobody says the subject.
S2.quote: If the loan buys a certificate nobody wants, that's my parents' savings gone too.
fieldNote: Worries most about his **parents' money**, not his own prospects.
Wants **collective**, government-led answers rather than personal workarounds.
Would **stay** at university mainly because leaving feels worse.

steps.text: Talk to my parents about whether the fees are worth it
Cut takeaways and the gym membership
Go to union meetings and push for a public plan
Write to our MP asking for written job guarantees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just enough time to be angry about it properly. I'd tell people on campus that we should be organising now, not waiting. Joining a union or a group like that is the sensible thing, instead of everyone panicking alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it gives me hope and fear together. I'd graduate around 2030, so the field might be wrecked right when I come out. But I'd have a few years to find something that can't be done by a machine, or to learn how to work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use summers for placements, probably in a hardware or electronics firm, since robots come later than thinking AI. I'd pay down some of my loan with the supermarket wages instead of spending them. And yes, I'd have to start learning the AI tools in third year, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More manageable than the two-year one. Five years feels like a storm forecast, scary but you can board up the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having three more years than the 2028 picture change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish the degree and not feel I've wasted it. In 2028 I'd be thinking about dropping out. In 2031 I'd be thinking about which module to pick, and that feels like a normal problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, but only for advice. The union, if it's real and not just posters. And my tutor Dr Mahmoud, who actually answers emails.

say: We should be **organising** now, not panicking alone later.
I'd tell people to join a **union** or a group like it.
think: The field might be **wrecked** just as I graduate in 2030.
I have time to find work **machines can't do** or learn to work with them.
do: Use summers for **hardware placements**, where robots arrive later.
Put some **supermarket wages** towards the loan.
Start learning **AI tools** in third year.
feel: **Manageable**, like a storm forecast where you can still board up the windows.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a storm forecast, scary but you can board up the windows.
fieldNote: The **extra time** moves him from thinking about dropping out to choosing modules.
Leans towards **hardware** and electronics, where robots arrive later.
Still wary of **AI tools**, but plans a late, practical step towards them.

steps.text: Pay 40 a month of wages towards the student loan
Learn the course's AI tools in third year
Join the student union's jobs and technology group
Pick electronics modules over pure software modules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it gives the country time to build proper safety nets, and I'd want that argued for loudly. At work, meaning the supermarket, I'd probably just say it's far off and we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I have time to choose well. I'd be 28 by 2036, maybe in a decent job by then, with savings. The worry is that the middle years are the dangerous ones, when firms start cutting and nobody has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and get a couple of years' real work, ideally somewhere that makes things. I'd keep up my habits and try the tools slowly, a bit each year. I'd also save properly, since by then I'd earn a real wage, and maybe put aside money for my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, but with a pit of worry underneath. Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast the last five years moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want done in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free retraining for anyone whose job is hit, and rules on firms before the change, not after. If we wait until it lands, it's the working people who pay, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be slow about AI by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. In ten years it'd be like refusing to use email. I'd still check the work, though, and I'd still write the first draft in my head before I let anything answer for me.

say: Ten years gives us time to build proper **safety nets**, and I'd argue for that loudly.
At the supermarket I'd just say it's **far off**.
think: I'd have time to **choose well** and save before it lands.
The **middle years** worry me most, when firms cut and nobody has a plan.
do: Finish the degree and get **two years** of real work at a firm that makes things.
Try AI tools **slowly**, a bit each year.
Save properly and set aside **money for my parents**.
feel: **Calm** on top, with a pit of worry underneath.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until you remember how fast the last five years moved.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **resistance** soften into a slow, practical habit.
Wants **rules** before the change, because working people pay when it comes late.
Plans to look after his **parents** with his future wages.

steps.text: Get two years of work at a manufacturing firm after graduating
Try one AI tool a year, checking its work myself
Vote and campaign for retraining funds before job losses
Set aside money for my parents' retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd still be at university, my dad would still be driving, and my parents would have spent real money on a degree. What would help is a clear public plan: retraining, protected jobs while it happens, and firms made to pay their share. Even a written promise would help me sleep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not as against technology as I probably sound. I'm against being told to keep up by people who profit when I do. If someone shows me how it helps without costing my dad his job, I'm listening.

headlineQuote: I'm against being told to keep up by people who profit when I do.
portrait: Pedro is an **18-year-old** computer engineering student from a bus-driver's family, with top results and a partial scholarship.
He distrusts hype, writes code on **paper first**, and never uses AI tools, but his resistance softens with a good reason.
He blames **firms and weak governments**, and turns to unions and public plans rather than personal tricks.
His fear peaks in the **2028 picture**, where his degree and parents' fees could be wasted, and eases with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: his degree and his parents' fees could be wasted.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **public plan** with retraining and protected jobs, plus firms made to pay their share.
